Written by Claude from the measurements above. An interpretation, not a measurement.

Barnard's Star is a small, cool red dwarf about 6 light-years away, and it moves across our sky faster than any other star. WANDERERS measured it shifting 170 arcseconds between 2010 and 2026, a speed of 10.55 arcseconds per year, within 1.5% of Gaia's 10.39. Confidence is high: all three key checks passed. The star is too bright for SPHEREx. All 242 measurements are flagged, so there is no reliable spectrum. Its brightness looked steady (−0.00 ± 0.04 mag), but that came only from the star's outer glow, so it's uncertain.

Sky Survey · NEOWISE 2014–2024 + SPHEREx 2025–26 · automated search
infrared detections, searched for anything that moves.

NASA's NEOWISE telescope photographed every part of the sky about every six months for ten years. We cut the sky into 12,288 equal tiles and, tile by tile, a program links each source's detections across the years, measures how far and how steadily it moves, throws out artefacts, and checks ESA's Gaia catalogue: a mover that Gaia already knows is explained. Then SPHEREx, which mapped the whole sky again in 2025–26, gets a say: the program reads SPHEREx's all-sky spectral cube at the spot where each unexplained mover should be by then, checks that it is there (and gone from where it was in 2014), and takes its 0.75–5 µm spectrum, looking for the methane dip and red colour of a cold brown dwarf. Whatever is left is ranked, so people can look at the most promising candidates first. A candidate is a lead, never a discovery.

NEOWISE measures the motion (2014–2024). SPHEREx has no source catalogue yet, so the program measures its DR1 cube directly; its ~13″ pixels confirm only fast motions (about 1″ a year or more) and can blend close neighbours.

What this search cannot tell you
Only the tiles listed here have been searched; the rest of the sky has not been processed yet.
Motions slower than 150 mas per year or faster than 12 arcseconds per year are not searched.
A source must be detected in at least 6 of the roughly 20 WISE visits, so very faint or very red objects near the detection limit can be missed.

'Unexplained' means no Gaia DR3 star with a matching motion lies within 3 arcseconds. That is expected for cold brown dwarfs too faint for Gaia, but blends, artefacts next to bright stars and tracks cut at tile edges can look the same.

A track that crosses a tile edge is split between the two tiles. When both parts are found and agree in position and motion they are counted once (the longer track is kept); a part too short to be found on its own is lost.
Motions come from a straight-line fit; parallax is fitted only where a value is given, so very nearby objects can have slightly biased motions.

SPHEREx has no public source catalogue yet; its check measures the all-sky DR1 spectral cube directly at each predicted position. Its pixels are about 13 arcseconds across, so it can only see motions of more than a few pixels over 2014-2026 (roughly 1 arcsecond per year and faster); slower movers can only be shown to be there. Two sources less than a pixel apart are blended, so a spectrum can include a neighbour's light.
A candidate is not a discovery: each one needs a human check of the images and other catalogues first.

"Unexplained" means only that Gaia DR3 has no matching moving star. Many such objects are already known from other surveys (brown dwarfs are too faint and cold for Gaia), and some are artefacts the cuts missed.
Only people looking at the images, then follow-up observations, can confirm anything new.
The run's own description of its method

Each processed tile holds every NEOWISE single-exposure detection from 2014 to 2024 (about 20 million per tile). Detections that fail basic quality cuts (artefact flags, bad frames, moonlight, weak signal) are dropped. WISE scanned each part of the sky about every six months, so the detections of one source in one scan are averaged into a single position per visit. Those positions are linked across the ten years into tracks, including fast movers of up to 12 arcseconds per year, and a straight-line fit gives each track's proper motion and its uncertainty. Tracks seen in at least 6 visits that move at least 150 mas per year with at least 5 sigma are kept as movers. Each mover is compared with Gaia DR3 stars moved to the same date with their own motion. Every mover Gaia does not explain is then looked up in SPHEREx's all-sky spectral cube (data release 1, observed 2025-26): is a source there, where its NEOWISE motion says it should be by then, and gone from where it was in 2014? SPHEREx also gives its 0.75-5 micron spectrum, from which a methane dip at 3.3 microns and a red 3-5 micron colour (signs of a cold brown dwarf) are read as hints. Movers are then ranked: those Gaia does not explain, that are red, that SPHEREx sees where predicted and that have long, clean tracks come first. The top of the list is for people to investigate.
